claims.text: The starting powder is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The mechanically processed powder has high surface energy.
Oxygen introduced during preparation can form TiO in a Ti-containing mechanically alloyed and SPS-consolidated alloy.
Ten hours of high-energy milling will produce chemical homogeneity and nanocrystalline refinement.
Mechanical alloying followed by SPS will suppress porosity and yield a dense bulk alloy.
SPS at 1100 °C, above 100 °C/min, and below five minutes dwell will stabilize a predominantly FCC solid solution with minor BCC.
Rapid SPS will kinetically suppress formation of brittle HCP phases.
A high heating rate and short dwell will limit the growth of TiO precipitates.
Controlling displacement or strain rate during sintering will minimize stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries act as vacancy sinks and thereby suppress porosity.
High configurational entropy stabilizes FCC against HCP transformation at the sintering temperature.
Milling-induced lattice distortion and defect density enhance sinterability and suppress porosity.
The processed alloy will have a grain size below 100 nm.
The processed alloy will exhibit hardness above 500 HV.
The processed alloy will have improved ductility relative to cast CoCrFeNiTi.
The rapidly sintered alloy will contain negligible HCP phase.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has porosity and a homogeneous but soft single-phase structure with low hardness.
Milling time affects contamination, and excessive milling can promote carbide or oxide contamination.
Sintering above 1200 °C will make grain coarsening and Laves-phase decomposition dominant.
Residual TiO precipitates could provide a competing precipitation-strengthening contribution or cause embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The rule says that increased HCP content or reduced hardness in the slow-heating or long-dwell controls would falsify the hypothesis. Those results would instead support the hypothesis that rapid heating and short dwell are essential. Only significant HCP or porosity in the rapid-SPS sample directly contradicts the stated prediction.

The hypothesis invokes both grain-boundary effects and solid-solution/lattice-distortion effects, but the proposed experiment does not independently vary grain size at fixed composition and phase content. It therefore cannot decisively distinguish grain-refinement hardness from solute strengthening.
